Adult Ocoee salamanders from the southern Blue Ridge attain a maximum snout–vent length of 5 centimeters [Li = 5 centimeters], a modest body size that aligns closely with the typical range reported for the Desmognathus ochrophaeus complex. This ultimate snout–vent length appears to be attained gradually over several years, reflecting the relatively slow growth trajectory characteristic of plethodontids occupying cool, headwater streams. Females engaging in reproduction produce clutches averaging 13 eggs [N_R_i = clutches averaging 13 eggs], although individual clutch sizes exhibit substantial variation, generally spanning from 5 to 23 eggs. Furthermore, reproductive effort is not an annual occurrence for most females; available data indicate that a typical breeding female produces a single clutch every other year [F_R_i = single clutch every other year]. This low-frequency reproductive schedule, combined with the modest clutch size, suggests a conservative life-history strategy adapted to the stable but resource-limited environments these salamanders inhabit, where energy allocation toward offspring is balanced against the demands of somatic maintenance and survival across multiple seasons.

The relatively small size of the adults is preceded by an equally modest beginning; newly hatched individuals emerge from their eggs weighing only 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams]. This exceptionally low birth mass is a direct consequence of the small egg diameter, which typically measures around 2.5 millimeters, though a range from 2 to 3 millimeters is commonly observed. Females deposit these yolk-laden eggs in concealed, moist microhabitats, such as beneath moss mats or within decaying logs, where the developing embryos undergo a prolonged incubation period. At a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time elapsed between oviposition and larval eclosion is approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days], a duration that can extend from 53 to 66 days depending on local thermal microclimates. This developmental timeline is typical of the genus and reflects the moderate metabolic rates associated with the cool, thermally stable groundwater seepages that form the preferred oviposition sites for Desmognathus species in the Appalachian region.

As the embryos complete their development at the same constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the emergence of the aquatic larva marks a critical transition from a yolk-dependent existence to an exotrophic feeding stage. During this period, the young salamander must begin actively foraging for small aquatic invertebrates to sustain its rapid growth. The transition to a feeding larva is followed by a prolonged period of somatic development before the animal reaches a state capable of reproduction. The time elapsed since birth at which sexual maturation occurs, again under those cool thermal conditions, is 511 days [tp = 511 days], or roughly 1.4 years after hatching. at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]This protracted period to reach puberty is consistent with the pattern observed in many desmognathine salamanders, where delayed reproduction is thought to enhance lifetime fitness by allowing individuals to achieve a sufficiently large body size before allocating resources to gamete production and the energetically demanding task of nest attendance.

The extended juvenile period delays first reproduction, but it also positions the species for a potentially lengthy adult tenure. Indeed, longevity records for the Ocoee salamander indicate a remarkable capacity for survival. When maintained under the same thermal conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum lifespan for this species has been recorded at approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], a duration that is notably high for a terrestrial salamander of this body size. This substantial longevity, combined with the iteroparous but infrequent reproductive schedule, implies that most reproductive output is concentrated in the later years of an individual's life. Such a life-history configuration is typical of species occupying stable but low-productivity montane habitats, where low adult mortality rates favor the evolution of delayed maturity and extended reproductive lifespans as mechanisms for ensuring population persistence. The total adult body mass that can be achieved over that long lifespan is up to 2 grams [Wwi = up to 2 grams].

The concordance between adult body mass, a maximum recorded value of 2 grams [Wwi = 2 grams], and the small body size at hatching underscores the profound ontogenetic shift that this species undergoes across its life cycle. The transition from a 0.0082 gram larva to a fully grown adult represents a several-hundred-fold increase in biomass, most of which occurs during the terrestrial juvenile and adult stages after metamorphosis. This pattern of growth, modulated by the cool perennial temperatures of southern Appalachian streams, generates a life history that combines small body size, delayed maturation, and exceptional longevity relative to body mass. When compared to other members of the Plethodontidae, the Ocoee salamander occupies an intermediate position in life-history space, balancing the high fecundity and rapid development of lowland species against the extreme longevity and low reproductive output of some fully terrestrial congeners. The ecological success of Desmognathus ocoee in its mosaic of rocky seeps and forested slopes is thus a direct product of these carefully traded-off life-history attributes.
